Spotify Premium.name: Spotify Premium
Spotify Premium.description: Spotify Premium is the paid tier of the world's most popular music streaming service. While the free tier is ad-supported with limited skips, Premium removes ads, enables offline downloads, and offers higher audio quality. At $11.99/month (Individual), it adds up to a significant annual cost for music lovers.
painPoints: Expensive: $11.99/month Individual, $16.99/month Duo, $19.99/month Family — adds up quickly
Free tier has unskipable ads every 2-3 songs, which is disruptive
Free tier limits skips (only 6 per hour on mobile)
Offline downloads are Premium-only — you can't listen without internet on free plan
HiFi lossless audio still hasn't fully rolled out despite being announced years ago
Artist payouts are controversially low (reportedly $0.003 – $0.005 per stream)
Spotify Premium.whySwitch: There are excellent free and cheaper alternatives for music streaming. YouTube Music (free tier) has no skip limits and includes music videos. SoundCloud (free) has exclusive tracks not on Spotify. For offline listening, purchasing music outright (Bandcamp) or self-hosting (Navidrome) gives you ownership. Many users also find that a well-curated local music library beats any streaming service.

Includes music videos, live sessions, and covers not on Spotify
Upload feature lets you add your own tracks to the cloud
Huge catalog — Google's metadata is excellent

Background play on mobile requires Premium (unless on Android with mod)
UI is less polished than Spotify
No collaborative playlists on free tier
alternatives.bestFor: Users who want a generous free tier and access to rare/live music content

Audio quality maxes out at 256kbps MP3 (no lossless)

migrationGuide.overview: Switching from Spotify Premium to an alternative depends on what you value most: if it's cost, YouTube Music free or SoundCloud free are good starting points. If it's ownership, Bandcamp lets you buy music outright. If it's privacy and control, Navidrome (self-hosted) is the answer.
steps: Export your Spotify playlists using a third-party tool like SpotMyBackup, Exportify, or TuneMyMusic
For YouTube Music: use TuneMyMusic or Soundiiz to transfer playlists directly
For Bandcamp: follow your favorite artists on Bandcamp and start purchasing albums — you'll get DRM-free downloads
For Navidrome: set up a server (NAS or VPS), organize your local music files, and install a Subsonic-compatible mobile app
Cancel Spotify Premium only after confirming your most-listened-to playlists are recreated elsewhere
Keep Spotify Free installed as a backup — you can still access your playlists with ads
tips: Use Soundiiz (free tier) or TuneMyMusic (free for 1 transfer) to move playlists between services — they support 50+ platforms
If you have local music files, Navidrome + Symfonium (Android) or play:Sub (iOS) gives you a Spotify-like experience with your own files
Bandcamp often has 'pay what you want' pricing — you can get full albums for $0 if the artist allows it
YouTube Music's upload feature is underrated — you can upload tracks not available on any streaming service and stream them from the cloud

faq.q: Will I lose my playlists if I cancel Spotify Premium?
faq.a: No — your playlists remain in your Spotify account even after canceling Premium (you just go back to the free ad-supported tier). However, downloaded offline music will stop working. Use Exportify or TuneMyMusic to back up your playlists before canceling.

faq.q: Is YouTube Music actually free (no skip limits)?
faq.a: Yes — YouTube Music's free tier lets you skip as many times as you want. The trade-off is ads (audio and video ads between songs). It's significantly more usable than Spotify's free tier, which limits skips.

faq.q: What about podcasts? Spotify has lots of exclusive podcasts.
faq.a: Most Spotify exclusive podcasts have moved to video (YouTube) or have RSS feeds you can use in any podcast app (Apple Podcasts, Pocket Casts, AntennaPod). YouTube Music also includes podcasts now. Very few podcasts are truly exclusive to Spotify anymore.

Adobe After Effects.name: Adobe After Effects
Adobe After Effects.description: Adobe After Effects is the industry-standard tool for motion graphics, visual effects (VFX), and compositing. It is a subscription-only product ($24.19/month standalone, or $62.99/month for all Creative Cloud apps). Many indie creators, YouTubers, and small studios find the subscription cost prohibitive.
painPoints: Expensive subscription: $24.19/month for After Effects alone, or $62.99/month for all Creative Cloud apps
Steep learning curve — overwhelming for beginners with hundreds of features
Resource-heavy — requires a powerful GPU and lots of RAM for smooth playback
No one-time purchase option — Adobe discontinued perpetual licenses
Frequent crashes on complex projects with many layers and effects
Adobe After Effects.whySwitch: High-quality alternatives now offer 80-90% of After Effects' capabilities at a fraction of the cost. Blender (free, open-source) has a powerful compositor and video editor built-in. DaVinci Resolve (free version is very capable) includes Fusion for motion graphics and VFX. For 2D motion graphics specifically, tools like OpenToonz (free) and Krita (free) are excellent. Even if you occasionally need After Effects, using alternatives for 80% of your work can dramatically reduce how many months you need to subscribe.

alternatives.name: Blender (Compositing & Video Editor)
features: Video Sequence Editor (VSE) for basic editing
pros: Completely free with no premium tiers — ever
Powerful compositor can handle many VFX tasks (keying, tracking, color grading)
Regular updates from the Blender Foundation
Excellent for 3D motion graphics (which After Effects can't do natively)
Open-source and privacy-friendly
cons: Not a direct 1:1 replacement for After Effects — different workflow
Compositor is powerful but less mature than After Effects for 2D motion graphics
Learning curve is steep for non-3D users
No native support for After Effects plugins or presets
alternatives.bestFor: 3D artists, motion designers who incorporate 3D, and budget-conscious creators

alternatives.name: DaVinci Resolve (Fusion page)
alternatives.pricing: Free version is very capable; Studio $295 one-time (not subscription!)
features: Fusion page for node-based compositing and motion graphics
Color page for professional color grading
Cut and Edit pages for video editing
Free version includes most features (limits: no noise reduction, limited resolution for some features)
pros: Free version is professional-grade — used in actual Hollywood films
One-time purchase for Studio ($295) vs Adobe's subscription forever model
Fusion is a true node-based compositor (like Nuke)
All-in-one: editing, color, VFX, audio in one app
Excellent color grading tools (industry-standard)
cons: Very steep learning curve — not beginner-friendly
Free version has some limitations (no AI tools, no some advanced features)
Resource-heavy — needs a powerful workstation
Not as many tutorials for Fusion as there are for After Effects
alternatives.bestFor: Professional video editors, colorists, and VFX artists who want an all-in-one solution

alternatives.name: Natron
features: OpenFX plugin support (many free and paid plugins available)
pros: Free and open-source — no cost whatsoever
Node-based workflow is similar to Nuke (good for learning professional VFX)
Supports many OpenFX plugins (some are free)
Lightweight compared to Blender or DaVinci Resolve
Good for learning compositing concepts without paying for software
cons: Development has slowed down in recent years (less active than Blender)
Smaller community than After Effects — fewer tutorials
Interface is functional but not as polished
Some advanced features are missing compared to After Effects or Nuke
alternatives.bestFor: Budget-conscious VFX artists and students learning node-based compositing

alternatives.name: OpenToonz (for 2D animation & motion graphics)
features: 2D animation software used by Studio Ghibli
Scan and clean-up tools for hand-drawn animation
pros: Completely free — used by major studios (Ghibli!)
Excellent for hand-drawn 2D animation and motion graphics
Open-source with active development
Unique features like the 'Effects' system for procedural animation
Good for traditional animators transitioning to digital
cons: Not a direct alternative for VFX/compositing (more for 2D animation)
Steep learning curve for the interface
Less suitable for live-action VFX than After Effects
Smaller plugin ecosystem than After Effects
alternatives.bestFor: 2D animators, hand-drawn motion graphics artists, and Studio Ghibli fans

alternatives.name: Krita (for 2D animation & motion graphics)
features: Excellent brush engine (great for frame-by-frame animation)
Good for motion graphics elements (titles, lower thirds)
pros: Free and open-source — no cost
Excellent for frame-by-frame 2D animation
Good brush engine for creating motion graphics assets
Active development and community
Can export animation as video or image sequence
cons: Not a VFX/compositing tool — more for creating assets
No node-based compositing like After Effects
Timeline is basic compared to dedicated video editors
Not suitable for complex VFX work
alternatives.bestFor: 2D animators and motion graphics artists creating frame-by-frame content

migrationGuide.overview: Migrating from After Effects to an alternative depends on what you use it for: 3D compositing (Blender), node-based VFX (Natron, Fusion), or 2D motion graphics (OpenToonz, Krita). The hardest part is re-creating your existing projects in the new tool.
steps: Identify your primary use case: VFX/compositing, 2D motion graphics, or 3D motion graphics
Download and install your chosen alternative (Blender for 3D, DaVinci Resolve for all-in-one, Natron for node-based compositing)
Follow beginner tutorials specifically for that alternative — don't try to map After Effects concepts 1:1
For existing projects, export assets (PNG sequences, video clips) from After Effects and import into the new tool
Re-create motion graphics templates from scratch in the new tool (there's no direct project conversion)
Cancel Adobe Creative Cloud subscription after confirming your workflow works in the alternative
Keep After Effects installed for a grace period in case you need to export old projects
tips: Blender's compositor is powerful but works differently than After Effects — watch Blender Guru or Blender Nation tutorials to learn the node-based workflow
DaVinci Resolve's Fusion page is the closest professional alternative to After Effects — if you can afford $295 one-time, it's worth it over subscription
For simple motion graphics (title animations, lower thirds), even Canva or CapCut can replace After Effects for 80% of use cases
If you only need After Effects occasionally, consider subscribing for 1 month, completing your project, then canceling — $24.19 for 1 month is cheaper than a year of subscription

faq.q: Can I open my After Effects project files (.aep) in these alternatives?
faq.a: No — there's no direct project file conversion. You need to render your After Effects compositions to video/PNG sequence, then import those assets into the new tool. For motion graphics templates, you'll need to re-create them from scratch in the alternative.

faq.q: What if I need to open After Effects project files that a client sent me?
faq.a: Ask the client to export the composition as a PNG sequence or video render with alpha channel. Alternatively, if they used specific plugins or effects, ask which ones — you might be able to recreate the look in your alternative. If you absolutely must open .aep files, consider subscribing to After Effects for 1 month to do the conversion.

faq.q: Is Blender a complete replacement for After Effects?
faq.a: For 3D motion graphics and compositing, Blender is actually superior (and free). For 2D motion graphics (title animations, shape animations, explainer videos), Blender's workflow is less intuitive than After Effects. For that use case, DaVinci Resolve (Fusion) or even Canva Pro might be a better fit depending on complexity.

Microsoft Visio.name: Microsoft Visio
Microsoft Visio.description: Microsoft Visio is a diagramming and vector drawing application for creating flowcharts, org charts, floor plans, network diagrams, and more. It is sold as a separate purchase from Microsoft 365: Visio Plan 1 starts at $5.00/user/month, Plan 2 at $15.00/user/month, and Visio Professional 2021 as a one-time purchase at $569.99.
painPoints: Expensive: $5–$15/user/month subscription, or $569.99 one-time (Professional 2021)
Not included in standard Microsoft 365 subscriptions — separate purchase required
Steep learning curve for advanced features (data-linked diagrams, custom stencils)
Windows-only (Visio for the web is limited compared to desktop version)
File format (.vsdx) creates vendor lock-in — hard to open in non-Microsoft tools
Microsoft Visio.whySwitch: Excellent free alternatives now match 90% of Visio's diagramming features. diagrams.net (draw.io) is completely free, runs in any browser, and supports Visio file import/export. Lucidchart (free tier) is excellent for collaboration. For technical diagrams (network, AWS architecture), tools like Miro and Excalidraw are modern and intuitive. For many users, Visio is overkill — a free web-based tool is all they need.

migrationGuide.overview: Migrating from Visio to an alternative is relatively straightforward because most modern diagramming tools support importing .vsdx files. The main work is adjusting formatting (fonts, colors, shape sizes) to match your organization's standards in the new tool.
steps: Identify which Visio features you actually use — basic flowcharts? data-linked diagrams? custom stencils?
Try importing your most complex .vsdx file into draw.io and Lucidchart to see which preserves formatting best
For each alternative, recreate your organization's standard templates and shape libraries
Set up integrations (Google Drive, OneDrive, GitHub) for file storage in the new tool
Share the new tool with your team and train them on the new interface
Export any Visio files you need to keep to .vsdx as backup before canceling Visio
tips: draw.io can import .vsdx files and export back to .vsdx — this is the best path if you occasionally need to share with Visio users
For AWS or Azure architecture diagrams, draw.io has excellent shape libraries for cloud infrastructure — often better than Visio's built-in stencils
If you use Visio for data-linked diagrams (linking shapes to Excel data), Lucidchart has a similar feature in its paid plan — test it before committing
Miro is excellent for early-stage diagramming (brainstorming, mind maps) but use draw.io for final, formal diagrams

faq.q: Can I open my existing .vsdx files in these alternatives?
faq.a: Yes — draw.io, Lucidchart, and some other tools support importing .vsdx files. Formatting may shift slightly (fonts, colors, shape sizes), so you'll need to do some cleanup. Export back to .vsdx is also supported in draw.io for sharing with Visio users.

faq.q: What if my organization requires Visio for compliance or standards?
faq.a: If your organization mandates Visio, you may need to keep a license. However, you can do the actual work in draw.io and export to .vsdx for delivery. This gives you the free tool's ease of use while maintaining compliance.

faq.q: Is there a truly offline alternative to Visio?
faq.a: Yes — draw.io has a desktop app (download from github.com/jgraph/drawio) that works completely offline. You can also use LibreOffice Draw (free, open-source) for simple diagrams, though it lacks the specialized shape libraries of Visio or draw.io.

TeamViewer.name: TeamViewer
TeamViewer.description: TeamViewer is a popular remote desktop and support tool that allows users to access computers and devices remotely for technical support, file transfer, and collaboration. While it has a free tier for personal use, commercial use requires a paid license starting at $24.90/month per user, with aggressive detection of commercial use that blocks free users.
painPoints: Free version aggressively detects 'commercial use' and blocks connections after a few minutes
Paid plans are expensive: $24.90/month per user (billed annually) for the basic business plan
Requires account creation and internet connection — no peer-to-peer without a server
Resource-heavy — can slow down older computers during remote sessions
Privacy concerns — TeamViewer has had security incidents, and the company can access connection metadata
TeamViewer.whySwitch: There are excellent free remote desktop tools that don't artificially limit free users. Chrome Remote Desktop is completely free with no time limits. AnyDesk (free for personal use) is faster and lighter than TeamViewer. For advanced users, Rustdesk (open-source, self-hostable) gives you complete control. Even Windows' built-in Remote Desktop (RDP) is free for Windows Pro users. For many use cases, TeamViewer is unnecessary expensive.

alternatives.name: Chrome Remote Desktop
alternatives.pricing: 100% free — no limits, no accounts beyond Google account
features: Browser-based — works in Chrome or Edge without installing desktop software (or use the Chrome Remote Desktop app)
Unattended access (set up permanent access to your computers)
File transfer via copy-paste through remote session
Cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS, Android, iOS)
pros: Completely free with no time limits or 'commercial use' detection
Works in browser — no complex setup or port forwarding
Google account security (2FA, security keys supported)
Very reliable — Google's infrastructure
Simple interface — easy for non-technical users
cons: Requires Google account (privacy concern for some)
No advanced features (no chat, no multi-monitor support in browser version)
File transfer is slow (copy-paste through remote session)
No mobile-to-mobile remote control (only remote into a desktop from mobile)
alternatives.bestFor: Personal use, simple remote access, and non-technical users

alternatives.name: AnyDesk

Simple interface — easier than TeamViewer for basic remote control

Privacy concerns similar to TeamViewer (connection routing through their servers)

pros: Completely free and open-source — no 'commercial use' restrictions
Self-hosting option gives you complete privacy and control
Lightweight and fast (Rust is efficient)

migrationGuide.overview: Migrating from TeamViewer to an alternative is straightforward — most alternatives have similar core features (remote control, file transfer, unattended access). The main work is setting up the new tool on all your devices and ensuring firewall/router settings allow connections.
steps: Choose your alternative based on your use case: Chrome Remote Desktop for personal/simple, AnyDesk for speed, Rustdesk for privacy, RDP for Windows-to-Windows
Install the alternative on all computers you need to access remotely
Set up unattended access (if needed) — this usually involves setting a fixed password or PIN
Test the connection from your typical remote locations (home, coffee shop, etc.) to ensure it works through firewalls
Update any documentation or shared credentials your team uses for remote access
Uninstall TeamViewer from all devices after confirming the new tool works reliably
tips: For Windows-to-Windows remote access over LAN, nothing beats built-in RDP for speed and quality — use it if both computers are on the same network
If you need to access computers over the internet without VPN, Chrome Remote Desktop is the simplest option (no port forwarding needed)
Rustdesk's self-hosted option is excellent for teams who want privacy and control — the Docker setup is well-documented
AnyDesk's 'TCP tunneling' feature lets you tunnel connections through AnyDesk (useful for accessing NAS or router admin pages remotely)

faq.q: Will the free alternatives suddenly block me for 'commercial use' like TeamViewer did?
faq.a: Chrome Remote Desktop and Rustdesk (self-hosted) have no 'commercial use' detection. AnyDesk's free version prohibits commercial use in its EULA, but it's not enforced by automatic detection like TeamViewer. For genuine commercial use, pay for a license — it's cheaper than TeamViewer.

faq.q: What about accessing my computer from a different network (no VPN)?
faq.a: Chrome Remote Desktop, AnyDesk, and Rustdesk (with their cloud relay) all work over the internet without VPN or port forwarding. Windows RDP requires either VPN or port forwarding (which has security risks). For secure internet-based RDP, set up a WireGuard VPN or use Chrome Remote Desktop instead.

faq.q: Is there a mobile app for remotely controlling my computer?
faq.a: Yes — Chrome Remote Desktop, AnyDesk, Rustdesk, and Microsoft Remote Desktop (iOS/Android) all have mobile apps. AnyDesk's mobile apps are particularly good — you can remotely control a PC from an iPad with a decent experience.

WinRAR.name: WinRAR
WinRAR.description: WinRAR is a popular file compression and archiving utility for Windows. It is shareware — you can use the trial version indefinitely, but it nags you to purchase a license ($29 for single-user) every time you open it. Many users tolerate the nag screen for years, not realizing there are excellent free alternatives.
painPoints: Nag screen every time you open WinRAR — asks you to buy a license even after the trial 'expires'
Cost: $29 for a single-user license (unnecessary when free alternatives exist)
Windows-only (no official macOS or Linux version)
Proprietary RAR format — people who receive .rar files may need WinRAR to open them (though 7-Zip can open RAR)
Lacks some modern features (encryption standards, archive formats) compared to newer tools
WinRAR.whySwitch: 7-Zip is a free, open-source file archiver that supports every format WinRAR does (including RAR extraction) and many more (7z, ZIP, GZIP, BZIP2, TAR, etc.). It's completely free with no nag screens, no registration, no ads. For macOS, Keka or The Unarchiver are excellent free alternatives. For most users, WinRAR is completely unnecessary — 7-Zip or the built-in Windows zip feature handles 99% of use cases.

alternatives.name: 7-Zip
features: Supports every major archive format: 7z, ZIP, GZIP, BZIP2, TAR, XZ, WIM, AR, CAB, DMG, ISO, RAR, and more
High compression ratio (especially with 7z format with LZMA/LZMA2)
Integration with Windows Shell (right-click context menu)
pros: Completely free with no ads, no nag screens, no registration
Open-source and actively maintained
Better compression than ZIP (7z format)
Handles RAR files (extract only — can't create RAR)
Lightweight — uses minimal system resources
Available in 80+ languages
cons: Interface is very dated (functional but not pretty)
No official support for creating RAR archives (but RAR is proprietary and dying anyway)
Windows-only (use p7zip on Linux/macOS)
No mobile app (but you can use ZArchiver on Android)
alternatives.bestFor: Windows users who want a free, powerful, no-nonsense file archiver

alternatives.name: PeaZip
features: Encrypted password manager for archive passwords
pros: Free and open-source with a more modern GUI than 7-Zip
Supports an incredible number of archive formats (200+)
Good security features (encrypted password manager, secure delete)
Portable version available (run from USB without installing)
Cross-platform (Windows and Linux)
cons: Slower compression speed than 7-Zip for some formats
Interface can feel cluttered with many options
Less widely known than 7-Zip (fewer tutorials online)
Windows-only for the official portable version (Linux uses different package)
alternatives.bestFor: Users who want a modern GUI and support for many archive formats

alternatives.name: The Unarchiver (macOS)
features: Supports every archive format you'll encounter (RAR, 7z, ZIP, TAR, GZIP, BZIP2, ISO, etc.)
Integrates with Finder — double-click any archive to extract
Also available as command-line tool (unar/lsar) for scripting
Supports non-UTF8 encoding (opens archives with Chinese/Japanese filenames correctly)
pros: Completely free with no ads
Just works — double-click any archive and it extracts
Handles filenames in any language correctly (unlike some other tools)
Very lightweight — doesn't slow down your Mac
Also works on older macOS versions
cons: macOS-only (not cross-platform)
No archive creation — only extraction (use Keka or 7-Zip for creating archives)
No GUI for advanced options (compression level, encryption) — use Keka for that
Development has slowed — it's stable but not actively adding features
alternatives.bestFor: Mac users who just need to extract archives (no creation needed)

alternatives.name: Keka (macOS)
alternatives.pricing: Free (with optional donation on website; Mac App Store version is $4.99)
features: .7z, ZIP, TAR, GZIP, BZIP2, XZ, LZIP, DMG, ISO
Split archives (split large files into multiple volumes)
Supports extracting RAR, 7z, ZIP, and many other formats
pros: Excellent macOS integration (much better than 7-Zip on Mac via Wine)
Free from website (donation optional); cheap on Mac App Store
Good compression ratios with 7z format
Handles split archives well
Clean, modern macOS-native interface
cons: macOS-only
Free version from website has a small nag screen (donation removes it; or buy from Mac App Store for $4.99 to remove entirely)
Not open-source (though free beer from website)
Fewer formats supported than PeaZip or 7-Zip
alternatives.bestFor: Mac users who want a native, full-featured compression tool

alternatives.name: Windows built-in ZIP support (no install needed)
features: Right-click any folder → 'Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder'
Double-click any .zip file to open and extract
pros: Already on your computer — no installation needed
Simple and familiar (every Windows user knows how to use it)
No ads, no nag screens, no registration
Good enough for 90% of users who only need ZIP (not RAR, 7z, etc.)
Fast for small to medium archives
cons: ZIP-only — can't create or extract 7z, RAR, TAR, etc.
No encryption options (no password-protected ZIP from right-click)
No advanced options (compression level, split archives)
Slower than 7-Zip for large archives
alternatives.bestFor: Casual users who only need ZIP compression/decompression

migrationGuide.overview: Migrating from WinRAR to a free alternative is the easiest migration possible — just install the alternative, and it will associate itself with archive file types. You can then uninstall WinRAR. Your existing .rar files can be opened by 7-Zip or PeaZip with no issues.
steps: Download and install 7-Zip (Windows) or Keka (macOS) — both are free
Open the alternative and use its 'Tools → Options → System' (7-Zip) to associate it with all archive formats
Double-click a .rar file to confirm the alternative opens it correctly
Uninstall WinRAR (optional — having multiple archivers doesn't hurt, but WinRAR's nag screen is annoying)
If you have any .rar files you created, consider re-compressing them to .7z format (better compression, open format)
Never see a WinRAR nag screen again
tips: 7-Zip's .7z format has better compression than RAR or ZIP — if you're creating archives, use 7z with LZMA2 for maximum compression
If you receive .rar files from others, 7-Zip extracts them perfectly — you don't need WinRAR for that
On macOS, The Unarchiver is the best free tool for extracting any archive format — it 'just works' with Finder
If you're tempted to buy WinRAR to stop the nag screen: don't. 7-Zip is free, open-source, and better in every way.

faq.q: Will I still be able to open .rar files if I uninstall WinRAR?
faq.a: Yes — 7-Zip, PeaZip, and The Unarchiver (macOS) all open .rar files perfectly. You don't need WinRAR to open RAR archives. The RAR compression format is proprietary, but the extraction algorithm has been reverse-engineered and is supported by all major free archivers.

faq.q: Should I still create .rar archives, or switch to something else?
faq.a: Switch to .7z (7-Zip) or .zip. 7z has better compression than RAR, is open-source (no proprietary format), and is supported by every major archiver. ZIP is the most compatible format (every OS can open ZIP natively). There's no reason to create .rar files anymore.

faq.q: Is 7-Zip safe? The website looks old and sketchy.
faq.a: Yes — 7-Zip is safe, open-source, and widely trusted. The website looks dated because the developer focuses on functionality over aesthetics. Download from the official site (7-zip.org) or via Microsoft Store / package managers (Chocolatey, winget, apt, etc.). It's been around since 1999 and is malware-free.
